quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Wolves and Rivers
quests.passage: When wolves were reintroduced to a large national park after seventy years of absence, ecologists expected the elk population to fall, and it did. What surprised them was what happened to the rivers. With fewer elk, and elk behaving more cautiously near open water where wolves could ambush them, willow and aspen seedlings along the banks began to survive. Taller vegetation stabilized the soil, and beavers, which depend on willows, returned to build dams. The dams created ponds, and the ponds provided habitat for fish, amphibians and nesting birds. Some scientists describe this chain of effects as a "trophic cascade" and cite it as evidence that predators shape landscapes. Others urge caution: the park also experienced a decade of unusually wet weather and a rise in bear numbers, both of which could have affected vegetation. The cascade, they say, is plausible but not proven, and the share of the recovery due to wolves alone remains uncertain.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: A Letter, Forty Years Late
quests.passage: Mrs. Whitcombe had retired a decade ago, and the envelope that arrived that Thursday bore a handwriting she did not recognize. Inside was a single page. "You may not remember me," it began. "I was the boy at the back who never finished anything. In your class in 1983 you wrote on my essay, 'Unfinished, but the unfinished part is the interesting part.' I have thought about that sentence for forty years. I am now a structural engineer, and I have a habit, which my colleagues find irritating, of asking what the unfinished part of every plan might be. It has saved us twice from serious mistakes. I wanted you to know." Mrs. Whitcombe read it standing in the hallway, then again at the kitchen table. She did remember the essay, though not the boy. For a long while she sat holding the page, and then she went to find a pen, because she felt that a letter like that deserved an answer, even a late one.

quests.passage: Opponents of the proposed $8 daily charge for driving into the city center call it a tax on the poor. The objection deserves a serious answer, and the answer begins with who actually drives there. Council data show that only 22 percent of commuters into the center arrive by car, and those who do have a median household income well above the city average. The majority arrive by bus, train or on foot, and they are currently stuck in the same traffic the cars create. The charge would raise an estimated $30 million a year, all of it earmarked for bus services. A fair critique would be that the plan lacks discounts for low-income drivers who have no alternative, and that is a reason to amend the proposal, not to abandon it. It is not a reason to keep a system in which the many subsidize the convenience of the few.

quests.passage: This policy covers loss or damage to your home and its contents caused by fire, storm, flood, theft and escape of water from pipes. Contents are covered up to $40,000 in total, with a limit of $2,500 for any single item unless you have listed it separately on your schedule. Damage caused by gradual wear, poor maintenance, or a failure to take reasonable care is not covered. For example, if a pipe bursts because it was not insulated during a freeze that you knew was forecast, we may reduce or decline your claim. If the home is left unoccupied for more than 30 consecutive days, cover for theft and escape of water is suspended unless you have told us in advance and we have agreed in writing. You must report theft to the police within 24 hours and give us the crime reference number. Claims for items worth more than $1,000 require proof of ownership, such as a receipt, photograph or valuation.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: The Island That Wasn't
quests.passage: For more than a century, maps and charts showed a stretch of land called Sandy Island in the Coral Sea. It was marked on British Admiralty charts in the 1870s and, later, in many atlases. In 2012, an Australian research vessel sailed to the position given and found only deep ocean, more than 1,300 meters deep. The ship's crew checked the charts again, then their instruments, and confirmed that nothing was there. Researchers later suggested that the island's origin was a whaling ship's report from 1876, which was copied from map to map without anyone checking it. Another possibility is that a floating raft of pumice, a volcanic stone that can drift for months, was mistaken for land. Whichever explanation is true, the episode shows how an error, once printed, can acquire authority simply by being repeated, and how rarely anyone returns to check the first source.

quests.passageTopic: Interview: A Farmer on a New Crop
quests.passage: Interviewer: You switched to sorghum three years ago. Was that a hard decision? Farmer: Not hard, but not simple either. My neighbors thought I was mad. Wheat is what this valley grows. But the last four summers have been dry, and wheat needs water at exactly the wrong time. Sorghum doesn't mind. It's an old crop in other countries, but around here people hadn't bothered with it for decades. Interviewer: So it was a purely financial decision? Farmer: I'd say it was a decision about risk. Sorghum earns less in a good year. In a bad year, it earns something, and wheat earns nothing. I'm not interested in a crop that makes me rich once and bankrupt twice. Interviewer: Have your neighbors changed their minds? Farmer: Two of them have planted a field each, "to experiment," they say. That's what we call it when we're not ready to admit someone else was right.

quests.passage: When my sister called to ask how the move had gone, I told her it was fine. The boxes had arrived, the movers had been kind, and the new flat had a view of a small park. "I'm sure you are," she said. "Saturday at noon, then." After we hung up, I looked at the stack of boxes labeled KITCHEN and realized I had been waiting, all week, for someone to ask exactly that question. For the first time since the move, I felt the flat might become home.

quests.passageTopic: Survey Summary: Remote Work at Calder & Ross
quests.passage: In a survey of 400 employees, 71 percent said they were more productive when working from home. Managers, however, were less convinced: only 38 percent of managers agreed that remote staff produced more. Output figures give a mixed picture. Teams that worked remotely three days a week completed 6 percent more tickets than office-based teams, but the average time to resolve customer complaints rose by one day. The survey also found that 54 percent of employees under thirty said they felt isolated from colleagues, compared with 19 percent of those over forty. The report concludes that remote work benefits individual task completion but may weaken collaboration and the support available to newer staff. It recommends a hybrid model of two office days a week, reviewed after six months, with additional mentoring for staff in their first year. The authors caution that the survey measures perceptions as well as results, and that the figures cover only one department.
